question.text: What should you do before any turn?

answer.text: Before any turn, check your mirrors, your surroundings and your blind spot, stay in your lane, signal your turn and yield the right-of-way.

teaching.text: Every turn starts with mirrors, surroundings and blind spot, then a signal and a yield. Remember: Check, stay in lane, signal, yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before any turn, check your mirrors, your surroundings and your blind spot, stay in your lane, signal your turn and yield the right-of-way.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Check, stay in lane, signal, yield

question.text: Why are last-second changes of plan dangerous before a turn?

answer.text: Last-second changes of plan are unsafe and can cause a crash, so check mirrors and the traffic behind you before turning into a side road or driveway.

teaching.text: Plan turns early, and check behind you before turning into a side road or driveway. Remember: Plan early; check behind first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Last-second changes of plan are unsafe and can cause a crash, so check mirrors and the traffic behind you before turning into a side road or driveway.

question.text: What must you avoid during a turn, and why give trucks and buses room?

answer.text: Do not change lanes in the middle of a turn or cut across the center line, and leave extra room for trucks and buses, which may swing over the center line as they turn.

teaching.text: Finish the turn in your own lane, and hang back while big vehicles swing wide. Remember: No lane changes; trucks swing wide.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not change lanes in the middle of a turn or cut across the center line, and leave extra room for trucks and buses, which may swing over the center line as they turn.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: No lane changes; trucks swing wide

question.text: A bus swings over the center line as it turns. May you do the same?

answer.text: Large trucks and buses may swing across the center line while turning, but you must not cross it yourself, so give them extra room instead.

teaching.text: A bus may cross the center line on a turn, but your car never should. Remember: Give room, keep your lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Large trucks and buses may swing across the center line while turning, but you must not cross it yourself, so give them extra room instead.

question.text: How do you set up a left turn at an intersection?

answer.text: For a left turn, check that your path is clear, keep near the center line, watch for pedestrians crossing on the left, and wait about halfway into the intersection while leaving room for oncoming turners.

teaching.text: Stay near the center line, watch the crosswalk on the left, and wait about halfway in. Remember: Clear path, near center, wait halfway.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a left turn, check that your path is clear, keep near the center line, watch for pedestrians crossing on the left, and wait about halfway into the intersection while leaving room for oncoming turners.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Clear path, near center, wait halfway

question.text: How should your wheels point while you wait to turn left, and why?

answer.text: While waiting to turn left, keep the steering wheel and wheels straight, because if you are hit from behind with the wheel turned left you will be pushed into oncoming traffic.

teaching.text: Straight wheels mean a rear-end hit pushes you forward, not into oncoming traffic. Remember: Wheels straight while waiting.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: While waiting to turn left, keep the steering wheel and wheels straight, because if you are hit from behind with the wheel turned left you will be pushed into oncoming traffic.

question.text: What is a U-turn, and is it always safe?

answer.text: A U-turn is one smooth U-shaped motion that reverses your direction, and it can be very dangerous even though some intersections allow it.

teaching.text: A U-turn sweeps across every lane in one motion, so it is risky even where allowed. Remember: One smooth motion; can be dangerous.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A U-turn is one smooth U-shaped motion that reverses your direction, and it can be very dangerous even though some intersections allow it.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: One smooth motion; can be dangerous

question.text: What should you check before making a U-turn?

answer.text: Before a U-turn, check all mirrors and traffic and look for any sign that prohibits it.

teaching.text: Mirrors, traffic and a quick look for a no-U-turn sign come first. Remember: Mirrors, traffic, no-U-turn signs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before a U-turn, check all mirrors and traffic and look for any sign that prohibits it.

question.text: When is a U-turn allowed on a rural two-lane highway?

answer.text: On any rural two-lane highway a U-turn is allowed as long as it is done safely and does not interfere with traffic.

teaching.text: Rural two-lane highways allow a U-turn if it is safe and does not interfere. Remember: Rural two-lane, if safe.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On any rural two-lane highway a U-turn is allowed as long as it is done safely and does not interfere with traffic.

question.text: How is a U-turn made, and where is it allowed unless a sign forbids it?

answer.text: A U-turn is a single continuous motion and is allowed on any rural two-lane highway when safe, unless a sign forbids it.

teaching.text: One continuous motion, allowed on rural two-lane roads unless a sign forbids it. Remember: Continuous turn, rural two-lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A U-turn is a single continuous motion and is allowed on any rural two-lane highway when safe, unless a sign forbids it.

question.text: With multiple turn lanes, which lane should you finish the turn in?

answer.text: With multiple turn lanes, finish the turn in the matching lane: start in the left-most lane and end in the left-most lane, start in the middle and end in the middle.

teaching.text: Left-most to left-most, middle to middle: finish in the lane that matches your start. Remember: End in the matching lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With multiple turn lanes, finish the turn in the matching lane: start in the left-most lane and end in the left-most lane, start in the middle and end in the middle.

question.text: From which lane must you turn right on a four-lane roadway?

answer.text: When turning right from a four-lane roadway, the turn must be made from the lane closest to the right curb or road edge.

teaching.text: On a four-lane road, right turns start from the lane nearest the curb. Remember: Right turn from the curb lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When turning right from a four-lane roadway, the turn must be made from the lane closest to the right curb or road edge.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Right turn from the curb lane

question.text: Where should you use a Y-turn, and where else will you be asked to do one?

answer.text: Use a Y-turn only in residential areas on streets too narrow for a U-turn; you will also be asked to perform one on the driving exam.

teaching.text: Save the Y-turn for narrow residential streets, and practice it for the driving exam. Remember: Narrow streets, and the exam.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use a Y-turn only in residential areas on streets too narrow for a U-turn; you will also be asked to perform one on the driving exam.

question.text: How does a Y-turn differ from a U-turn?

answer.text: A Y-turn is a stop-and-reverse turnaround reserved for residential streets too narrow for a U-turn, and it is also a graded maneuver on the driving exam.

teaching.text: A Y-turn stops and reverses; a U-turn never does. Remember: Stop, reverse, narrow streets.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A Y-turn is a stop-and-reverse turnaround reserved for residential streets too narrow for a U-turn, and it is also a graded maneuver on the driving exam.

question.text: What is the first step of a Y-turn?

answer.text: Y-turn step one: signal right, check your mirrors and the traffic on your right, move over as far to the right as possible, and stop.

teaching.text: First, signal right, pull far right and stop. Remember: Signal right, move right, stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Y-turn step one: signal right, check your mirrors and the traffic on your right, move over as far to the right as possible, and stop.

question.text: What is the second step of a Y-turn?

answer.text: Y-turn step two is to signal left, check your blind spot, turn left across to the opposite curb and stop.

teaching.text: Second, signal left, check your blind spot, cross to the opposite curb and stop. Remember: Signal left, cross, stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Y-turn step two is to signal left, check your blind spot, turn left across to the opposite curb and stop.

question.text: What are the third and fourth steps of a Y-turn?

answer.text: Y-turn step three is to look back over your right shoulder and reverse just far enough to drive forward again, then stop; step four is to check left and right and pull forward into your lane.

teaching.text: Third, look back and reverse just enough; fourth, check both ways and pull forward. Remember: Look back, reverse, then forward.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Y-turn step three is to look back over your right shoulder and reverse just far enough to drive forward again, then stop; step four is to check left and right and pull forward into your lane.

question.text: Which step of the Y-turn is the only one where you reverse?

answer.text: In the Y-turn the only reversing step is the third one, where you look back over your right shoulder before backing.

teaching.text: Only step three goes backward. Remember: Step three reverses.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In the Y-turn the only reversing step is the third one, where you look back over your right shoulder before backing.

question.text: When may you use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle?

answer.text: You may use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle only when that vehicle is stopped or is making a left turn.

teaching.text: The shoulder is only for getting around a stopped or left-turning vehicle. Remember: Only past stopped or left-turners.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You may use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle only when that vehicle is stopped or is making a left turn.

question.text: Which lane is for going around slower vehicles on a multi-lane road, and why is passing on the right risky?

answer.text: On a multi-lane road the left-most lane is the lane for going around slower vehicles, and passing on the right is risky because the other driver may not see you.

teaching.text: Pass in the left-most lane; the right side is where drivers may not see you. Remember: Left lane passes; right is risky.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a multi-lane road the left-most lane is the lane for going around slower vehicles, and passing on the right is risky because the other driver may not see you.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Left lane passes; right is risky

question.text: How does a normal pass differ from going around on the shoulder?

answer.text: Passing on the left is the normal pass, while going around on a paved shoulder is allowed only past a stopped or left-turning vehicle.

teaching.text: The left lane is the normal pass; the shoulder is the narrow exception. Remember: Pass left; shoulder rarely.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing on the left is the normal pass, while going around on a paved shoulder is allowed only past a stopped or left-turning vehicle.

question.text: What should you do when another driver is passing you?

answer.text: If another driver is trying to pass you, keep to your lane and slow down.

teaching.text: When someone passes you, hold your lane and ease off the gas. Remember: Keep your lane, slow down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If another driver is trying to pass you, keep to your lane and slow down.

question.text: What must you do before changing lanes?

answer.text: Before changing lanes, make sure the way is clear, signal first, move only one lane at a time, and look over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward.

teaching.text: Clear, signal, one lane at a time, and a look over your shoulder. Remember: Clear, signal, one lane, shoulder check.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before changing lanes, make sure the way is clear, signal first, move only one lane at a time, and look over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Clear, signal, one lane, shoulder check

question.text: What are blind spots, and how do you check them?

answer.text: The areas you check over your left and right shoulders are blind spots, which cannot be seen by using your mirrors alone.

teaching.text: Blind spots sit beside you where mirrors cannot reach. Remember: Over-the-shoulder zones mirrors miss.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The areas you check over your left and right shoulders are blind spots, which cannot be seen by using your mirrors alone.

question.text: Why are mirrors not enough before a lane change?

answer.text: Checking mirrors is not enough before a lane change, because the blind spots are seen only by looking over the shoulder toward the new lane.

teaching.text: Only a head turn toward the new lane reveals the blind spot. Remember: Shoulder check sees blind spots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Checking mirrors is not enough before a lane change, because the blind spots are seen only by looking over the shoulder toward the new lane.

question.text: How many vehicles may you pass at once, and on which side?

answer.text: Pass only one vehicle at a time and only on the left, since there may not be time to get around several vehicles or even the one ahead of you.

teaching.text: One vehicle at a time, always on the left. Remember: One vehicle, on the left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pass only one vehicle at a time and only on the left, since there may not be time to get around several vehicles or even the one ahead of you.

question.text: May you stay in the passing lane or speed up to finish a pass?

answer.text: Do not linger in the passing lane, and never exceed the speed limit to complete a pass.

teaching.text: Do not linger beside the other car, and never speed to finish. Remember: No lingering, no speeding.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not linger in the passing lane, and never exceed the speed limit to complete a pass.

question.text: What room do you need before passing, and must others move over?

answer.text: Pass only when there is enough room in front of the vehicle you are passing, and remember that other drivers are not required to move over for you.

teaching.text: Pass only with clear room ahead, and do not expect anyone to move over. Remember: Room ahead; nobody must move.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pass only when there is enough room in front of the vehicle you are passing, and remember that other drivers are not required to move over for you.

question.text: Does passing change the speed limit or require the other driver to move over?

answer.text: The speed limit still applies while passing, and the vehicle being passed has no duty to move over for you.

teaching.text: The limit stands while passing, and the other driver owes you no room. Remember: Limit stands; no duty to move.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The speed limit still applies while passing, and the vehicle being passed has no duty to move over for you.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Limit stands; no duty to move

question.text: When is it safe to return to the driving lane after passing?

answer.text: It is safe to return to the driving lane once both headlights of the vehicle you passed appear in your rearview mirror.

teaching.text: Wait for both headlights in your rearview mirror before moving back. Remember: Both headlights in the mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: It is safe to return to the driving lane once both headlights of the vehicle you passed appear in your rearview mirror.

question.text: What cue tells you it is safe to move back after passing?

answer.text: After passing, the cue that it is safe to move back into the driving lane is seeing both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.

teaching.text: Alongside is too soon; both headlights in the mirror is the cue. Remember: See both headlights first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After passing, the cue that it is safe to move back into the driving lane is seeing both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.

question.text: How far and how fast should you back up?

answer.text: Because it is hard to see behind a vehicle, back up as little as possible and no faster than a slow walk.

teaching.text: Keep backing short and no faster than a slow walk. Remember: Little and at walking pace.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Because it is hard to see behind a vehicle, back up as little as possible and no faster than a slow walk.

question.text: How should you look when backing, besides mirrors and a camera?

answer.text: When backing, do not rely only on your mirrors and backup camera: turn your body, look over your right shoulder through the rear window, and use a helper outside the car when you can.

teaching.text: Turn and look back through the rear window instead of trusting the camera alone. Remember: Turn, look back, use a helper.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When backing, do not rely only on your mirrors and backup camera: turn your body, look over your right shoulder through the rear window, and use a helper outside the car when you can.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Turn, look back, use a helper

question.text: What should you do after backing, and what if you miss an exit?

answer.text: After backing, scan left and right before rejoining traffic, and if you miss an exit or turn, never back up; continue to the next exit and come back.

teaching.text: Scan both ways after backing, and never reverse toward a missed exit. Remember: Scan, and never back up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After backing, scan left and right before rejoining traffic, and if you miss an exit or turn, never back up; continue to the next exit and come back.

question.text: You miss your highway exit. What do you do?

answer.text: A missed exit is handled by driving to the next exit and coming back, never by backing up on the road.

teaching.text: Missed it? Go to the next exit and come back. Remember: Next exit, then come back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A missed exit is handled by driving to the next exit and coming back, never by backing up on the road.

question.text: Where should you normally park so your car is not a hazard?

answer.text: You are responsible for making sure your parked vehicle is not a hazard, which normally means parking on the far-right side, clear of any travel lane.

teaching.text: Park far right, fully out of the travel lanes. Remember: Far right, out of lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You are responsible for making sure your parked vehicle is not a hazard, which normally means parking on the far-right side, clear of any travel lane.

question.text: Where is parking not allowed?

answer.text: Parking is not allowed along yellow-marked curbs, in front of fire hydrants, or where a No Parking sign is posted.

teaching.text: Yellow curbs, hydrants and No Parking signs mean no parking. Remember: Yellow curbs, hydrants, no-parking signs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parking is not allowed along yellow-marked curbs, in front of fire hydrants, or where a No Parking sign is posted.

question.text: How should you park on level ground?

answer.text: Park at a very low speed, and on level ground shift into Park, or into gear with a manual transmission, and set the parking brake.

teaching.text: On level ground, use Park or a gear, and set the parking brake. Remember: Park or gear, brake set.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Park at a very low speed, and on level ground shift into Park, or into gear with a manual transmission, and set the parking brake.

question.text: Which way do you turn the wheels when parked uphill with a curb?

answer.text: Parked uphill with a curb, turn the wheels all the way to the left before shifting into park.

teaching.text: Uphill against a curb, the wheels go all the way left. Remember: Uphill with curb: left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parked uphill with a curb, turn the wheels all the way to the left before shifting into park.

question.text: Which way do you turn the wheels when parked uphill without a curb?

answer.text: Parked uphill without a curb, turn the wheels all the way to the right before shifting into park.

teaching.text: Uphill with no curb, the wheels go all the way right. Remember: Uphill, no curb: right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parked uphill without a curb, turn the wheels all the way to the right before shifting into park.

question.text: Which way do you turn the wheels when parked downhill, and what else do you set?

answer.text: Parked downhill, turn the wheels all the way to the right, and on any hill set the emergency brake.

teaching.text: Downhill, the wheels go right, and every hill gets the emergency brake. Remember: Downhill right; brake on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parked downhill, turn the wheels all the way to the right, and on any hill set the emergency brake.

question.text: Which hill-parking case turns the wheels left, and which cases turn them right?

answer.text: Uphill with a curb is the left-wheel case, while uphill without a curb and every downhill park are right-wheel cases.

teaching.text: Ask one question: uphill with a curb? Then left; otherwise right. Remember: Curb uphill left; else right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Uphill with a curb is the left-wheel case, while uphill without a curb and every downhill park are right-wheel cases.

question.text: What should you watch for, and how big a space do you need, to parallel park?

answer.text: For parallel parking between vehicles, watch for traffic, pedestrians and fixed objects, and look for a space about three-six feet longer than your vehicle.

teaching.text: Look for a space a few feet longer than your car, and watch for people and objects. Remember: Space a bit longer than car.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For parallel parking between vehicles, watch for traffic, pedestrians and fixed objects, and look for a space about three-six feet longer than your vehicle.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Space a bit longer than car

question.text: How does parallel parking begin?

answer.text: Parallel parking starts with your turn signal on and a stop alongside the vehicle ahead of the space, about two feet away from it.

teaching.text: Signal and stop beside the car ahead, about two feet away. Remember: Signal, stop beside, small gap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parallel parking starts with your turn signal on and a stop alongside the vehicle ahead of the space, about two feet away from it.

question.text: How does the starting gap compare with the extra length of the space?

answer.text: When you begin parallel parking you stop about two feet from the car ahead, and the space you choose should be about three-six feet longer than your car.

teaching.text: The small gap is beside the car ahead; the extra length is the space itself. Remember: Small gap beside, longer space.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you begin parallel parking you stop about two feet from the car ahead, and the space you choose should be about three-six feet longer than your car.

question.text: What is the next step after stopping beside the car ahead?

answer.text: Next, turn the wheel fully toward the side you are parking on, left for the left side of the road and right for the right side, and back up slowly.

teaching.text: Turn the wheel fully toward your parking side and back slowly. Remember: Turn fully toward curb, back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Next, turn the wheel fully toward the side you are parking on, left for the left side of the road and right for the right side, and back up slowly.

question.text: When do you straighten the wheel while backing into a parallel space?

answer.text: When your front door passes the rear bumper of the car you are parking behind, straighten the wheel and keep backing slowly in a straight line.

teaching.text: When your front door reaches their rear bumper, straighten and keep backing. Remember: Door passes bumper, straighten.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When your front door passes the rear bumper of the car you are parking behind, straighten the wheel and keep backing slowly in a straight line.

question.text: When do you turn the wheel the other way while parallel parking?

answer.text: Once your bumper clears the vehicle in front, turn the wheel sharply the other way and back slowly until you are parallel to the curb.

teaching.text: Once your bumper clears the car in front, swing the wheel the other way. Remember: Bumper clears, turn opposite.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Once your bumper clears the vehicle in front, turn the wheel sharply the other way and back slowly until you are parallel to the curb.

question.text: How do you finish a parallel park, and what distances should you end with?

answer.text: Finish by straightening the wheels, ending about a foot from the curb and at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.

teaching.text: End with straight wheels, a foot from the curb and room from the other cars. Remember: Foot from curb, room around.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Finish by straightening the wheels, ending about a foot from the curb and at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.

question.text: How does the final curb distance compare with the distance from other vehicles?

answer.text: At the end of a parallel park you should be about a foot from the curb, but at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.

teaching.text: The curb gets about a foot; the other cars get at least two feet. Remember: Close to curb, room between cars.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At the end of a parallel park you should be about a foot from the curb, but at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Close to curb, room between cars

question.text: How do you let other drivers know where you are and what you plan?

answer.text: Let other drivers know where you are and what you intend by using headlights, brakes, turn signals and hazard lights, and by keeping space ahead and behind.

teaching.text: Lights, brakes, signals, hazards and steady space all tell others your plans. Remember: Lights, signals, space speak.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Let other drivers know where you are and what you intend by using headlights, brakes, turn signals and hazard lights, and by keeping space ahead and behind.

question.text: Should you drive when you are very upset or excited?

answer.text: Strong emotions affect safe driving, so do not drive when you are very worried, excited, afraid, angry or depressed.

teaching.text: If you are very upset or excited, wait before you drive. Remember: Calm first, then drive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Strong emotions affect safe driving, so do not drive when you are very worried, excited, afraid, angry or depressed.

question.text: What are a light tap and a hard press of the horn for?

answer.text: The horn exists to help prevent crashes: a light tap gets another driver's attention, and a hard press warns of a collision about to happen.

teaching.text: The horn is a safety tool: a tap to alert, a hard press to warn. Remember: Tap alerts, press warns.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The horn exists to help prevent crashes: a light tap gets another driver's attention, and a hard press warns of a collision about to happen.

question.text: How does a light horn tap differ from a hard press?

answer.text: A light tap on the horn is for getting attention, while a hard press is reserved for warning of an imminent collision.

teaching.text: A tap gets attention; a hard press means a crash is about to happen. Remember: Attention versus danger.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A light tap on the horn is for getting attention, while a hard press is reserved for warning of an imminent collision.

question.text: Why use low beams, and what should you know if they switch on automatically?

answer.text: Low beams help you see and be seen; even if your car switches them on automatically, learn the manual control and check that they come on when needed.

teaching.text: Even with automatic headlights, know the manual switch and check it works. Remember: Learn the manual switch.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Low beams help you see and be seen; even if your car switches them on automatically, learn the manual control and check that they come on when needed.

question.text: When are low beams required?

answer.text: Low beams are required when you cannot see a vehicle or person five hundred feet away, about one block, and from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise.

teaching.text: The law requires low beams after dark and whenever you cannot see five hundred feet. Remember: Short view, or after dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Low beams are required when you cannot see a vehicle or person five hundred feet away, about one block, and from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise.

question.text: When are low beams recommended?

answer.text: Low beams are recommended whenever your windshield wipers are on and in rain, snow or fog.

teaching.text: Wipers on, rain, snow or fog: low beams are recommended. Remember: Wipers on, rain, snow, fog.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Low beams are recommended whenever your windshield wipers are on and in rain, snow or fog.

question.text: Which low-beam situations are required, and which are only recommended?

answer.text: Low beams are required at the five hundred-foot visibility threshold and in the half hour after sunset through the half hour before sunrise, but are only recommended with wipers on or in rain, snow or fog.

teaching.text: Darkness and short visibility require them; weather and wipers recommend them. Remember: Dark required; wipers recommended.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Low beams are required at the five hundred-foot visibility threshold and in the half hour after sunset through the half hour before sunrise, but are only recommended with wipers on or in rain, snow or fog.

question.text: When should you use high beams, and when must you dim them?

answer.text: High beams let you see twice as far as low beams; use them when no vehicles are approaching or in an unfamiliar place or construction area, and dim them for oncoming traffic.

teaching.text: High beams double your view on empty roads; dim them for oncoming traffic. Remember: Brights when clear; dim oncoming.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: High beams let you see twice as far as low beams; use them when no vehicles are approaching or in an unfamiliar place or construction area, and dim them for oncoming traffic.

question.text: What should you do about an oncoming driver's high beams, and when are parking lights used?

answer.text: If an oncoming driver leaves the high beams on, look toward the right side of the road, and use parking lights only while parked and idling.

teaching.text: Glance to the right edge to avoid glare, and keep parking lights for parked and idling. Remember: Look right; parking lights parked.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If an oncoming driver leaves the high beams on, look toward the right side of the road, and use parking lights only while parked and idling.

question.text: How do high beams differ from parking lights in when they are used?

answer.text: High beams double your seeing distance compared with low beams, yet must be dimmed when a vehicle approaches; parking lights are only for when you are parked and idling.

teaching.text: High beams are for driving on empty roads; parking lights are for standing still. Remember: Brights driving; parking lights parked.

question.text: In what order do you signal and move, and how early do you signal before an intersection turn?

answer.text: Turn on your signal, check around you, and then move; at an intersection, begin signaling about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, before the turn.

teaching.text: Signal, check, move, starting about three seconds before an intersection turn. Remember: Signal, check, then move.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn on your signal, check around you, and then move; at an intersection, begin signaling about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, before the turn.

question.text: When your turn comes just after an intersection, when do you signal?

answer.text: When your turn comes just after an intersection, wait until you have crossed the intersection before signaling.

teaching.text: For a driveway just past the corner, cross first and then signal. Remember: Cross first, then signal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When your turn comes just after an intersection, wait until you have crossed the intersection before signaling.

question.text: How does signal timing differ for a turn at an intersection and a turn just past one?

answer.text: At an intersection you signal about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, ahead of the turn, but for a turn just past an intersection you wait until you have crossed it.

teaching.text: Early signal for the corner, delayed signal for the turn beyond it. Remember: Early before; after crossing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At an intersection you signal about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, ahead of the turn, but for a turn just past an intersection you wait until you have crossed it.

question.text: When may hand signals replace turn signals, and what are the three signals?

answer.text: Hand signals may replace turn signals that are missing or hard to see: arm straight out the driver window to turn left, elbow bent with the hand up to turn right, and hand pointed down to slow or stop.

teaching.text: When turn signals fail, use your left arm out the driver window. Remember: Straight left, up right, down stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand signals may replace turn signals that are missing or hard to see: arm straight out the driver window to turn left, elbow bent with the hand up to turn right, and hand pointed down to slow or stop.

question.text: Which arm position means a left turn, a right turn, and slowing or stopping?

answer.text: In hand signals a straight arm means a left turn, an arm bent upward means a right turn, and an arm pointed down means slowing or stopping.

teaching.text: Straight out for left, bent up for right, pointed down for slow or stop. Remember: Straight, bent up, pointed down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In hand signals a straight arm means a left turn, an arm bent upward means a right turn, and an arm pointed down means slowing or stopping.

hooks_spoken: Check mirrors and blind spot, stay in your lane, signal and yield before every turn.
Give trucks and buses room as they swing wide, but never cross the center line yourself.
Wait halfway into the intersection with your wheels straight before a left turn.

hooks_spoken: A U-turn is one smooth motion, allowed on rural two-lane highways when safe and not forbidden.
Finish multi-lane turns in the matching lane, and turn right from the curb lane.
A Y-turn is for narrow residential streets, and only its third step reverses.

hooks_spoken: Pass on the left, one vehicle at a time, and use the shoulder only around stopped or left-turning cars.
Check blind spots over your shoulder before a lane change.
Never speed to pass, and return when both headlights show in your mirror.

hooks_spoken: Back up little, slowly, looking over your shoulder.
Never back up for a missed exit.
Uphill with a curb, wheels left; every other hill, wheels right.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of backing and parking on hills. Back up little, slowly, looking over your shoulder. Never back up for a missed exit. Uphill with a curb, wheels left; every other hill, wheels right. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Choose a space a few feet longer than your car and start beside the car ahead.
Turn fully, straighten as your door passes the bumper, then turn the other way.
Finish about a foot from the curb with room ahead and behind.

hooks_spoken: Use lights, signals and space to show other drivers your plans, and drive calm.
Tap the horn for attention; press it hard to warn of a crash.
Low beams are required when your view is short and after dark, and recommended with wipers on.
